entries.54b85139f4b536fa7be7a7619ff57c5c5f1510d9: <div sID="gen13210" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="144" osisID="Ps.144" sID="Ps.144"/> <div eID="gen13210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13211" type="x-p"/> The four preceding psalms seem to have been penned by David before his accession to the crown, when he was persecuted by Saul; this seems to have been penned afterwards, when he was still in trouble (for there is no condition in this world privileged with an exemption from trouble), the neighbouring nations molesting him and giving him disturbance, especially the Philistines, <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.17">2 Sam. v. 17</reference>. In this psalm, I. He acknowledges, with triumph and thankfulness, the great goodness of God to him in advancing him to the government , <reference osisRef="Ps.144.1-Ps.144.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. He prays to God to help him against the enemies who threatened him, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.5-Ps.144.8">ver. 5-8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.144.11">again ver. 11</reference>. III. He rejoices in the assurance of victory over them, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.9-Ps.144.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>. IV. He prays for the prosperity of his own kingdom, and pleases himself with the hopes of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.12-Ps.144.15">ver. 12-15</reference>. In singing this psalm we may give God the glory of our spiritual privileges and advancements, and fetch in help from him against our spiritual enemies; we may pray for the prosperity of our souls, of our families, and of our land; and, in the opinion of some of the Jewish writers, we may refer the psalm to the Messiah and his kingdom.
entries.c50043276ccb1b36906147bcde5eb241b84342eb: <div eID="gen13211" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Grateful Acknowledgments of Divine Goodness; Prayer for Success against Enemies.</title> <div sID="gen13212" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> my strength, which teacheth my hands to war, <hi type="italic">and</hi> my fingers to fight: <hi type="super">2</hi> My goodness, and my fortress; my high tower, and my deliverer; my shield, and <hi type="italic">he</hi> in whom I trust; who subdueth my people under me. <hi type="super">3</hi> <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , what <hi type="italic">is</hi> man, that thou takest knowledge of him! <hi type="italic">or</hi> the son of man, that thou makest account of him! <hi type="super">4</hi> Man is like to vanity: his days <hi type="italic">are</hi> as a shadow that passeth away. <hi type="super">5</hi> Bow thy heavens, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , and come down: touch the mountains, and they shall smoke. <hi type="super">6</hi> Cast forth lightning, and scatter them: shoot out thine arrows, and destroy them. <hi type="super">7</hi> Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children; <hi type="super">8</hi> Whose mouth speaketh vanity, and their right hand <hi type="italic">is</hi> a right hand of falsehood. <div eID="gen13212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13213" type="x-p"/> Here, I. David acknowledges his dependence upon God and his obligations to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.1-Ps.144.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. A prayer for further mercy is fitly begun with a thanksgiving for former mercy; and when we are waiting upon God to bless us we should stir up ourselves to bless him. He gives to God the glory of two things:— <div eID="gen13213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13214" type="x-p"/> 1. What he was to him: <hi type="italic">Blessed be the Lord my</hi> rock (<reference osisRef="Ps.144.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">my goodness, my fortress,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.144.2">v. 2</reference>. He has in the covenant engaged himself to be so, and encouraged us, accordingly, to depend upon him; all the saints, who by faith have made him theirs, have found him not only to answer but to out do their expectations. David speaks of it here as the matter of his trust, and that which made him easy, as the matter of his triumph, and that which made him glad, and in which he gloried. See how he multiplies words to express the satisfaction he had in God and his interest in him. (1.) "He is <hi type="italic">my strength,</hi> on whom I stay, and from whom I have power both for my work and for my warfare, my rock to build on, to take shelter in." Even when we are weak we may <hi type="italic">be strong in the Lord and in the power of his might.</hi> (2.) "<hi type="italic">My goodness,</hi> not only good to me, but my chief good, in whose favour I place my felicity, and who is the author of all the goodness that is in me, and <hi type="italic">from whom comes every good and perfect gift.</hi>" (3.) "<hi type="italic">My fortress,</hi> and <hi type="italic">my high tower,</hi> in whom I think myself as safe as ever any prince thought himself in a castle or strong-hold." David had formerly sheltered himself in strong-holds at En-gedi (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.29">1 Sam. xxiii. 29</reference>), which perhaps were natural fastnesses. He had lately made himself master of the strong-hold of Zion, which was fortified by art, and he <hi type="italic">dwelt in the fort</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.7">2 Sam. v. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.9">9</reference>), but he depends not on these. "Lord," says he, "thou art <hi type="italic">my fortress</hi> and <hi type="italic">my high tower.</hi>" The divine attributes and promises are fortifications to a believer, far exceeding those either of nature or art. (4.) <hi type="italic">My deliverer,</hi> and, as it is in the original, very emphatically, <hi type="italic">my deliverer to me,</hi> "not only a deliverer I have interest in, but who is always nigh unto me and makes all my deliverances turn to my real benefit." (5.) "<hi type="italic">My shield,</hi> to guard me against all the malignant darts that my enemies let fly at me, not only <hi type="italic">my fortress</hi> at home, but <hi type="italic">my shield</hi> abroad in the field of battle." Wherever a believer goes he carries his protection along with him. <hi type="italic">Fear not, Abram, I am thy shield.</hi> <div eID="gen13214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13215" type="x-p"/> 2. What he had done for him. He was bred a shepherd, and seems not to have been designed by his parents, or himself for any thing more. But, (1.) God had made him a soldier. His hands had been used to the crook and his fingers to the harp, but God <hi type="italic">taught his hands to war and his fingers to fight,</hi> because he designed him for Israel's champion; and what God calls men to he either finds them or makes them fit for. Let the men of war give God the glory of all their military skill; the same that teaches the meanest husbandman his art teaches the greatest general his. It is a pity that any whose fingers God has taught to fight should fight against him or his kingdom among men. Those have special reason to acknowledge God with thankfulness who prove to be qualified for services which they themselves never thought of. (2.) God had made him a sovereign prince, had taught him to wield the sceptre as well as the sword, to rule as well as fight, the harder and nobler art of the two: He <hi type="italic">subdueth my people under me.</hi> The providence of God is to be acknowledged in making people subject to their prince, and so preserving the order and benefit of societies. There was a special hand of God inclining the people of Israel to be subject to David, pursuant to the promise God had made him; and it was typical of that great act of divine grace, the bringing of souls into subjection to the Lord Jesus and making them willing in the day of his power. <div eID="gen13215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13216" type="x-p"/> II. He admires God's condescension to man and to himself in particular (<reference osisRef="Ps.144.3-Ps.144.4">v. 3, 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Lord, what is man,</hi> what a poor little thing is he, <hi type="italic">that thou takest knowledge of him, that thou makest account of him,</hi> that he falls so much under thy cognizance and care, and that thou hast such a tender regard to any of that mean and worthless race as thou hast had to me!" Considering the many disgraces which the human nature lies under, we have reason to admire the honours God has put upon mankind in general (the saints especially, some in a particular manner, as David) and upon the Messiah (to whom those words are applied, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.6">Heb. ii. 6</reference>), who was <hi type="italic">highly exalted because he humbled himself to be found in fashion as a man,</hi> and <hi type="italic">has authority to execute judgment because he is the Son of man.</hi> A question to this purport David asked (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.4">Ps. viii. 4</reference>), and he illustrated the wonder by the consideration of the great dignity God has placed man in (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.5">Ps. viii. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou hast crowned him with glory and honour.</hi> Here he illustrates it by the consideration of the meanness and mortality of man, notwithstanding the dignity put upon him (<reference osisRef="Ps.144.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Man is like to vanity;</hi> so frail is he, so weak, so helpless, compassed about with so many infirmities, and his continuance here so very short and uncertain, that he is as like as may be to vanity itself. Nay, he is vanity, he is so at his best estate. <hi type="italic">His days</hi> have little substance in them, considering how many of the thoughts and cares of an immortal soul are employed about a poor dying body; they <hi type="italic">are as a shadow,</hi> dark and flitting, transitory and finishing with the sun, and, when that sets, resolving itself into all shadow. They <hi type="italic">are as a shadow that passeth away,</hi> and there is no loss of it. David puts himself into the number of those that are thus mean and despicable. <div eID="gen13216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13217" type="x-p"/> III. He begs of God to strengthen him and give him success against the enemies that invaded him, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.5-Ps.144.8">v. 5-8</reference>. He does not specify who they were that he was in fear of, but says, <hi type="italic">Scatter them, destroy them.</hi> God knew whom he meant, though he did not name them. But afterwards he describes them (<reference osisRef="Ps.144.7-Ps.144.8">v. 7, 8</reference>): "They are <hi type="italic">strange children,</hi> Philistines, aliens, bad neighbours to Israel, heathens, whom we are bound to be strange to and not to make any leagues with, and who therefore carry it strangely towards us." Notwithstanding the advantages with which God had blessed David's arms against them, they were still vexatious and treacherous, and men that one could put no confidence in: "One cannot take their word, for their <hi type="italic">mouth speaketh vanity;</hi> nay, if they give their hand upon it, or offer their hand to help you, there is no trusting them; for <hi type="italic">their right hand is a right hand of falsehood.</hi>" Against such as these we cannot defend ourselves, but we may depend on the God of truth and justice, who hates falsehood, to defend us from them. 1. David prays that God would appear, that he would do something extraordinary, for the conviction of those who preferred their dunghill-deities before the God of Israel (<reference osisRef="Ps.144.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Bow thy heavens, O Lord!</hi> and make it evident that they are indeed thine, and that thou art the Lord of them, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.1">Isa. lxvi. 1</reference>. Let thy providence threaten my enemies, and look black upon them, as the clouds do on the earth when they are thick, and hang very low, big with a storm. Fight against those that fight against us, so that it may visibly appear that thou art for us. <hi type="italic">Touch the mountains,</hi> our strong and stately enemies, <hi type="italic">and</hi> let them <hi type="italic">smoke.</hi> Show thyself by the ministry of thy angels, as thou didst upon Mount Sinai." 2. That he would appear against his enemies, that he would fight from heaven against them, as sometimes he had done, by lightnings, which are his arrows (his fiery darts, against which the hardest steel is no armour of proof, so penetrating is the force of lightning), that he himself would shoot these arrows, who, we are sure, never misses his mark, but hits where he aims. 3. That he would appear for him, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.7">v. 7</reference>. He begs for their destruction, in order to his own deliverance and the repose of his people: "<hi type="italic">Send thy hand,</hi> thy power, <hi type="italic">from above,</hi> for that way we look for help; <hi type="italic">rid me and deliver me out of</hi> these <hi type="italic">great waters</hi> that are ready to overflow me." God's time to help his people is when they are sinking and all other helps fail.
entries.1a28726e0ec577a4987d7890b9516b3b169972ef: <div eID="gen13217" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Thanksgiving and Petitions; National Happiness Desired.</title> <div sID="gen13218" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> I will sing a new song unto thee, O God: upon a psaltery <hi type="italic">and</hi> an instrument of ten strings will I sing praises unto thee. <hi type="super">10</hi> <hi type="italic">It is he</hi> that giveth salvation unto kings: who delivereth David his servant from the hurtful sword. <hi type="super">11</hi> Rid me, and deliver me from the hand of strange children, whose mouth speaketh vanity, and their right hand <hi type="italic">is</hi> a right hand of falsehood: <hi type="super">12</hi> That our sons <hi type="italic">may be</hi> as plants grown up in their youth; <hi type="italic">that</hi> our daughters <hi type="italic">may be</hi> as corner stones, polished <hi type="italic">after</hi> the similitude of a palace: <hi type="super">13</hi> <hi type="italic">That</hi> our garners <hi type="italic">may be</hi> full, affording all manner of store: <hi type="italic">that</hi> our sheep may bring forth thousands and ten thousands in our streets: <hi type="super">14</hi> <hi type="italic">That</hi> our oxen <hi type="italic">may be</hi> strong to labour; <hi type="italic">that there be</hi> no breaking in, nor going out; that <hi type="italic">there be</hi> no complaining in our streets. <hi type="super">15</hi> Happy <hi type="italic">is that</hi> people, that is in such a case: <hi type="italic">yea,</hi> happy <hi type="italic">is that</hi> people, whose God <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen13218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13219" type="x-p"/> The method is the same in this latter part of the psalm as in the former; David first gives glory to God and then begs mercy from him. <div eID="gen13219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13220" type="x-p"/> I. He praises God for the experiences he had had of his goodness to him and the encouragements he had to expect further mercy from him, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.9-Ps.144.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. In the midst of his complaints concerning the power and treachery of his enemies, here is a holy exultation in his God: <hi type="italic">I will sing a new song to thee, O God!</hi> a song of praise for new mercies, for those compassions that are new every morning. Fresh favours call for fresh returns of thanks; nay, we must praise God for the mercies we hope for by his promise as well as those we have received by his providence, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.20-2Chr.20.21">2 Chron. xx. 20, 21</reference>. He will join music with his songs of praise, to express and excite his holy joy in God; he will praise God <hi type="italic">upon a psaltery of ten strings,</hi> in the best manner, thinking all little enough to set forth the praises of God. He tells us what this new song shall be (<reference osisRef="Ps.144.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">It is he that giveth salvation unto kings.</hi> This intimates, 1. That great kings cannot save themselves without him. Kings have their life-guards, and have armies at command, and all the means of safety that can be devised; but, after all, it is God that gives them their salvation, and secures them by those means, which he could do, if there were occasion, without them, <reference osisRef="Ps.33.16">Ps. xxxiii. 16</reference>. Kings are the protectors of their people, but it is God that is their protector. How much service do they owe him then with their power who gives them all their salvations! 2. That good kings, who are his ministers for the good of their subjects, shall be protected and saved by him. He has engaged to give salvation to those kings that are his subjects and rule for him; witness the great things he had done for <hi type="italic">David his servant,</hi> whom he had many a time <hi type="italic">delivered from the hurtful sword,</hi> to which Saul's malice, and his own zeal for the service of his country, had often exposed him. This may refer to Christ the Son of David, and then it is a new song indeed, a New-Testament song. God delivered him from the hurtful sword, upheld him as his servant, and brought him off a conqueror over all the powers of darkness, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Isa. xlii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.8">xlix. 8</reference>. To him he gave salvation, not for himself only, but for us, raising him up to be <hi type="italic">a horn of salvation.</hi> <div eID="gen13220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13221" type="x-p"/> II. He prays for the continuance of God's favour. <div eID="gen13221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13222" type="x-p"/> 1. That he might be delivered from the public enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.11">v. 11</reference>. Here he repeats his prayer and plea, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.7-Ps.144.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. His persecutors were still of the same character, false and perfidious, and who would certainly over-reach an honest man and be too hard for him: "Therefore, Lord, do thou <hi type="italic">deliver me from</hi> them, for they are a strange sort of people." <div eID="gen13222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13223" type="x-p"/> 2. That he might see the public peace and prosperity: "Lord, let us have victory, that we may have quietness, which we shall never have while our enemies have it in their power to do us mischief." David, as a king, here expresses the earnest desire he had of the welfare of his people, wherein he was a type of Christ, who provides effectually for the good of his chosen. We have here, <div eID="gen13223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13224" type="x-p"/> (1.) The particular instances of that public prosperity which David desired for his people. [1.] A hopeful progeny (<reference osisRef="Ps.144.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">That our sons</hi> and <hi type="italic">our daughters may be</hi> in all respects such as we could wish." He means not those only of his own family, but those of his subjects, that are the seed of the next generation. It adds much to the comfort and happiness of parents in this world to see their children promising and likely to do well. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is pleasant to see <hi type="italic">our sons as plants grown up in their youth,</hi> as olive-plants (<reference osisRef="Ps.128.1-Ps.128.6">Ps. cxxviii. 3</reference>), the <hi type="italic">planting of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Isa. lxi. 3</reference>),—to see them as plants, not as weeds, not as thorns,—to see them as plants growing great, not withered and blasted,—to see them of a healthful constitution, a quick capacity, a towardly disposition, and especially of a pious inclination, likely to bring forth fruit unto God in their day,—to see them <hi type="italic">in their youth,</hi> their growing time, increasing in every thing that is good, growing wiser and better, till they grow strong in spirit. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is no less desirable to see <hi type="italic">our daughters as corner-stones,</hi> or corner-pillars, <hi type="italic">polished after the similitude of a palace,</hi> or temple. By daughters families are united and connected, to their mutual strength, as the parts of a building are by the corner-stones; and when they are graceful and beautiful both in body and mind they are then polished after the similitude of a nice and curious structure. When we see our daughters well-established and stayed with wisdom and discretion, as corner-stones are fastened in the building,—when we see them by faith united to Christ, as the chief corner-stone, adorned with the graces of God's Spirit, which are the polishing of that which is naturally rough, and <hi type="italic">become women professing godliness,</hi>—when we see them purified and consecrated to God as living temples, we think ourselves happy in them. [2.] Great plenty. Numerous families increase the care, perhaps more than the comfort, where there is not sufficient for their maintenance; and therefore he prays for a growing estate with a growing family. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That their store-houses might be well-replenished with the fruits and products of the earth: <hi type="italic">That our garners may be full,</hi> like those of the good householder, who brings out of them things new and old (those things that are best new he has in that state, those that are best when they are kept he has in that state),—that we may have in them <hi type="italic">all manner of stores,</hi> for ourselves and our friends,—that, living plentifully, we may live not luxuriously, for then we abuse our plenty, but cheerfully and usefully,—that, having abundance, we may be thankful to God, generous to our friends, and charitable to the poor; otherwise, what profit is it to have our garners full? <reference osisRef="Jas.5.3">Jam. v. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That their flocks might greatly increase: <hi type="italic">That our sheep may bring forth thousands, and ten thousands, in our</hi> folds. Much of the wealth of their country consisted in their flocks (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.26">Prov. xxvii. 26</reference>), and this is the case with ours too, else wool would not be, as it is, a staple commodity. The increase of our cattle is a blessing in which God is to be acknowledged. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That their beasts designed for service might be fit for it: <hi type="italic">That our oxen may be strong to labour</hi> in the plough, <hi type="italic">that they may be fat and fleshy</hi> (so some), in good working case. We were none of us made to be idle, and therefore we should pray for bodily health, not that we may be easy and take our pleasures, but that we <hi type="italic">may be strong to labour,</hi> that we may do the work of our place and day, else we are worse than the beasts; for when they are strong it is for labour. [3.] An uninterrupted peace. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That there be no war, <hi type="italic">no breaking in</hi> of invaders, <hi type="italic">no going out</hi> of deserters. "Let not our enemies break in upon us; let us not have occasion to march out against them." War brings with it abundance of mischiefs, whether it be offensive or defensive. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That there be no oppression nor faction—<hi type="italic">no complaining in our streets,</hi> that the people may have no cause to complain either of their government or of one another, nor may be so peevish as to complain without cause. It is desirable thus to dwell in quiet habitations. <div eID="gen13224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13225" type="x-p"/> (2.) His reflection upon this description of the prosperity of the nation, which he so much desired (<reference osisRef="Ps.144.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Happy are the people that are in such a case</hi> (but it is seldom so, and never long so), <hi type="italic">yea, happy are the people whose God is the Lord.</hi> The relation of a people to God as theirs is here spoken of either, [1.] As that which is the fountain whence all those blessings flow. Happy are the Israelites if they faithfully adhere to the Lord as their God, for they may expect to be <hi type="italic">in such a case.</hi> National piety commonly brings national prosperity; for nations as such, in their national capacity, are capable of rewards and punishments only in this life. Or, [2.] As that which is abundantly preferable to all these enjoyments. The psalmist began to say, as most do, <hi type="italic">Happy are the people that are in such a case;</hi> those are blessed that prosper in the world. But he immediately corrects himself: <hi type="italic">Yea, rather, happy are the people whose God is the Lord,</hi> who have his favour, and love, and grace, according to the tenour of the covenant, though they have not abundance of this world's goods. As all this, and much more, cannot make us happy, unless the Lord be our God, so, if he be, the want of this, the loss of this, nay, the reverse of this, cannot make us miserable.  <chapter eID="Ps.144"/> <div eID="gen13225" type="x-p"/>

entries.00009ce4fa10381b48238a69a097a0db8453490d: <chapter n="144" osisID="Ps.144" sID="Ps.144"/><div eID="gen10906" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7113"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 144</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.144.1-Ps.144.15">Psa 144:1-15</reference>. David's praise of God as his all-sufficient help is enhanced by a recognition of the intrinsic worthlessness of man. Confidently imploring God's interposition against his enemies, he breaks forth into praise and joyful anticipations of the prosperity of his kingdom, when freed from vain and wicked men.</title> <div sID="gen10907" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Ps.144"/>

entries.fc195a7344ecd3dd83c3f2d68dd3d53fe3648de2: <div eID="gen23447" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23448" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23449" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23449" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23448" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23450" type="x-p"/> The psalmist praises God for his goodness, <reference osisRef="Psa.144.1">Psa 144:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.144.2">Psa 144:2</reference>. Exclamations relative to the vanity of human life, <reference osisRef="Psa.144.3">Psa 144:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.144.4">Psa 144:4</reference>. He prays against his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.144.5-Psa.144.8">Psa 144:5-8</reference>; and extols God's mercy for the temporal blessings enjoyed by his people, <reference osisRef="Psa.144.9-Psa.144.15">Psa 144:9-15</reference>. <div eID="gen23450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23451" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew, and all the Versions, attribute this Psalm to David. The Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic, term it, A Psalm of David against Goliath. The Syriac says, "A Psalm of David when he slew Asaph, the brother of Goliath." Calmet thinks, and with much probability, that it was composed by David after the death of Absalom, and the restoration of the kingdom to peace and tranquillity. From a collation of this with Psalm 18, of which it appears to be an abridgment, preserving the same ideas, and the same forms of expression, there can be no doubt of both having proceeded from the same pen, and that David was the author. There is scarcely an expression here of peculiar importance that is not found in the prototype; and for explanation I must refer generally to the above Psalm. <div eID="gen23451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23452" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23453" type="x-p"/> Teacheth my hands to war - To use sword, battle-axe, or spear. <div eID="gen23453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23454" type="x-p"/> And my fingers to fight - To use the bow and arrows, and the sling.
entries.b3d8f260882728cff00c8ba4703c683d29db78fa: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23455" type="x-p"/> Who subdueth my people - Who has once more reduced the nation to a state of loyal obedience. This may refer to the peace after the rebellion of Absalom.
entries.b0d7ea5fbf69b5d3a6efb2db523f1d4c816c85df: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23456" type="x-p"/> Lord, what is man - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Psa.8.4">Psa 8:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.8.5">Psa 8:5</reference>. What is Adam, that thou approvest of him? Can he do any thing worthy of thy notice? Or the son of feeble perishing man, that thou shouldest hold him in repute? What care, love, and attention, dost thou lavish upon him!
entries.8812f555aa8d6b668c96c6fc8a4b803f8f20c6d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23457" type="x-p"/> Man is like to vanity - אדם להבל דמה Adam lahebel damah, literally, Adam is like to Abel, exposed to the same miseries, accidents, and murderers; for in millions of cases the hands of brothers are lifted up to shed the blood of brothers. What are wars but fratricide in the great human family? <div eID="gen23457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23458" type="x-p"/> His days are as a shadow - The life of Abel was promissory of much blessedness; but it afforded merely the shadow of happiness. He was pure and holy, beloved of his parents, and beloved of God; but, becoming the object of his brother's envy, his life became a sacrifice to his piety.
entries.f9404a240456f22f695c36f93a624d2e0346afad: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23459" type="x-p"/> Bow thy heavens - See the note on <reference osisRef="Psa.18.9">Psa 18:9</reference>.
entries.311b5499b2508d1f6919aa0f8f4af965f3fc1a57: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23460" type="x-p"/> Cast forth lightning - See the note <reference osisRef="Psa.18.13-Psa.18.14">Psa 18:13-14</reference> (note).
entries.fa39bbdc7b7e3a1bd2e39f44daa5d7d2aa1c6a2d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23461" type="x-p"/> Deliver me out of great waters - See the note <reference osisRef="Psa.18.16">Psa 18:16</reference>.
entries.b583ace8b433be434c7ccd36cf92f3d0ee40b3e7: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen23461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23462" type="x-p"/> I will sing a new song - A song of peculiar excellence. I will pour forth all my gratitude, and all my skill, on its composition. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.33.2">Psa 33:2</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Psa.33.3">Psa 33:3</reference> (note).
entries.4bdd77f1a3cf7432efe92921c55d93a2ea778fd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen23462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23463" type="x-p"/> He that giveth salvation unto kings - Monarchy, in the principle, is from God: it is that form of government which, in the course of the Divine providence, has principally prevailed; and that which, on the whole, has been most beneficial to mankind. God, therefore, has it under his peculiar protection. It is by him that kings reign; and by his special providence they are protected.
entries.b7408cd92390d7a0a712cd7bed3a382f502d9f63: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen23463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23464" type="x-p"/> That our sons may be as plants - God had promised to his people, being faithful, Three descriptions of Blessings, <reference osisRef="Deu.28.4">Deu 28:4</reference>. <div eID="gen23464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23465" type="x-p"/> 1. The fruit of the body - sons and daughters. <div eID="gen23465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23466" type="x-p"/> 2. The fruits of the ground - grass and corn in sufficient plenty. <div eID="gen23466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23467" type="x-p"/> 3. Fruit of the cattle-"the increase of kine, and flocks of sheep." <div eID="gen23467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23468" type="x-p"/> These are the blessings to wnich the psalmist refers here, as those in which he might at present exult and triumph: blessings actually enjoyed by his people at large; proofs of his mild and paternal government, and of the especial blessing of the Almighty. The people who there in such a state, and revolted, had no excuse: they were doubly guilty, as ungrateful both to God and man.
entries.739bf7dad9d912cfb4ccb32f6be5a4c9bca87696: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen23468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23469" type="x-p"/> That our garners, etc. - Our garners are full. These are not prayers put up by David for such blessings: but assertions, that such blessings were actually in possession. All these expressions should be understood in the present tense. <div eID="gen23469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23470" type="x-p"/> Ten thousands in our streets - בחצתינו bechutsotheynu should be translated in our pens or sheep-walks; for sheep bringing forth in the streets of cities or towns is absurd.
entries.a468d9d89e4e7e512e16698993baadcd0fabf834: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen23470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23471" type="x-p"/> Our oxen may be strong to labor - We have not only an abundance of cattle; but they are of the most strong and vigorous breed. <div eID="gen23471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23472" type="x-p"/> No breaking in - So well ordered is the police of the kingdom, that there are no depredations, no robbers, house-breakers, or marauding parties, in the land; no sudden incursions of neighboring tribes or banditti breaking into fields or houses, carrying away property, and taking with them the people to sell them into captivity: there is no such breaking in, and no such going out, in the nation. My enemies are either become friends, and are united with me in political interests; or are, through fear, obliged to stand aloof.
entries.75b6dcb84a3b598f0365641252c91fc1166915f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen23472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23473" type="x-p"/> Happy is that people - "O how happy are the people!" Such were his people; and they had not only all this secular happiness, but they had Jehovah for their God; and in him had a ceaseless fountain of strength, protection, earthly blessings, and eternal mercies! A people in such a case to rebel, must have the curse of God and man.  <chapter eID="Ps.144"/> <div eID="gen23473" type="x-p"/>

entries.399d64c1187eb458f1dae59ce5a7bf0a062ead1f: <div eID="gen10314" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Taking Courage in God before a Decisive Combat</title> <div sID="gen10315" type="x-p"/> Praised be Jahve who teacheth me to fight and conquer (<reference osisRef="Ps.144.1">Psa 144:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.2">Psa 144:2</reference>), me the feeble mortal, who am strong only in Him, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.3">Psa 144:3</reference>-4. May Jahve then be pleased to grant a victory this time also over the boastful, lying enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.5-Ps.144.8">Psa 144:5-8</reference>; so will I sing new songs of thanksgiving unto Him, the bestower of victory, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.9">Psa 144:9</reference>-10. May He be pleased to deliver me out of the hand of the barbarians who envy us our prosperity, which is the result of our having Jahve as our God, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.11">Psa 144:11</reference>-15. A glance at this course of the thought commends the additional inscription of the lxx (according to Origen only “in a few copies”), πρὸς τὸν Γολιάδ, and the Targumist’s reference of the “evil sword” in <reference osisRef="Ps.144.10">Psa 144:10</reference> to the sword of Goliath (after the example of the Midrash). Read 1Sa 17:47. The Psalm has grown out of this utterance of David. In one of the old histories, just as several of these lie at the foundation of our Books of Samuel as sources of information that are still recognisable, it was intended to express the feelings with which David entered upon the single-handed combat with Goliath and decided the victory of Israel over the Philistines. At that time he had already been anointed by Samuel, as both the narratives which have been worked up together in the First Book of Samuel assume: see <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.13">1Sa 16:13</reference>; 1Sa 10:1. And this victory was for him a gigantic stride to the throne. <div eID="gen10315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10316" type="x-p"/> If אשׁר in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.144.12">Psa 144:12</reference></hi> is taken as <hi type="italic">eo quod</hi>, so that envy is brought under consideration as a motive for the causeless (שׁוא), lyingly treacherous rising (ימין שׁקר) of the neighbouring peoples, then the passage <reference osisRef="Ps.144.12-Ps.144.15">Psa 144:12-15</reference> can at any rate be comprehended as a part of the form of the whole. But only thus, and not otherwise; for אשׁר cannot be intended as a statement of the aim or purpose: in order that they may be...(Jerome, De Wette, Hengstenberg, and others), since nothing but illustrative substantival clauses follow; nor do these clauses admit of an optative sense: We, whose sons, may they be...(Maurer); and אשׁר never has an assuring sense (Vaihinger). It is also evident that we cannot, with Saadia, go back to <reference osisRef="Ps.144.9">Psa 144:9</reference> for the interpretation of the אשׁר (Arab. <hi type="italic">asbh 'lâ mâ</hi>). But that junction by means of <hi type="italic">eo quod</hi> is hazardous, since envy or ill-will (קנאה) is not previously mentioned, and וימינם ימין שׁקר expresses a fact, and not an action. If it is further considered that nothing is wanting in the way of finish to the Psalm if it closes with <reference osisRef="Ps.144.11">Psa 144:11</reference>, it becomes all the more doubtful whether <reference osisRef="Ps.144.12-Ps.144.15">Psa 144:12-15</reference> belonged originally to the Psalm. And yet we cannot discover any Psalm in its immediate neighbourhood to which this piece might be attached. It might the most readily, as Hitzig correctly judges, be inserted between <reference osisRef="Ps.147.13">Psa 147:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.147.14">Psa 147:14</reference> of Ps 147. But the rhythm and style differ from this Psalm, and we must therefore rest satisfied with the fact that a fragment of another Psalm is here added to <reference osisRef="Ps.144.1-Ps.144.15">Psa 144:1-15</reference>, which of necessity may be accounted as an integral part of it; but in spite of the fact that the whole Psalm is built up on a gigantic scale, this was not its original corner-stone, just as one does not indeed look for anything further after the refrain, together with the mention of David in Psa 144:10., cf. Ps 18:51.
entries.090ab4d0716bcccfba727c88fb5d4c6de2898aba: <reference osisRef="Ps.144.1-Ps.144.2">Psa 144:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen10316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10317" type="x-p"/> The whole of this first strophe is an imitation of David’s great song of thanksgiving, Ps 18. Hence the calling of Jahve “my rock,” <reference osisRef="Ps.18.3">Psa 18:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.47">Psa 18:47</reference>; hence the heaping up of other appellations in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.144.2">Psa 144:2</reference></hi>, in which <reference osisRef="Ps.18.3">Psa 18:3</reference> is echoed; but וּמפלּטי־לי (with Lamed deprived of the <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>) follows the model of 2Sa 22:2. The naming of Jahve with חסדּי is a bold abbreviation of אלהי חסדּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.59.11">Psa 59:11</reference>, 18, as also in <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.8">Jon 2:8</reference> the God whom the idolatrous ones forsake is called הסדּם. Instead of מלחמה the Davidic Psalms also poetically say קרב, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.22">Psa 55:22</reference>, cf. Psa 78:9. The expression “who traineth my hands for the fight” we have already read in Psa 18:35. The last words of the strophe, too, are after <reference osisRef="Ps.18.48">Psa 18:48</reference>; but instead of ויּדבּר this poet says הרודד, from רדד = רדה (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.45.1">Isa 45:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.2">Isa 41:2</reference>), perhaps under the influence of uwmoriyd in 2Sa 22:48. In <reference osisRef="Ps.18.48">Psa 18:48</reference> we however read עמּים, and the Masora has enumerated <reference osisRef="Ps.144.2">Psa 144:2</reference>, together with <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.44">2Sa 22:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.14">Lam 3:14</reference>, as the three passages in which it is written עמי, whilst one expects עמים (ג דסבירין עמים), as the Targum, Syriac, and Jerome (yet not the lxx) in fact render it. But neither from the language of the books nor from the popular dialect can it be reasonably expected that they would say עמּי for עמּים in such an ambiguous connection. Either, therefore, we have to read עמים,<note placement="foot">Rashi is acquainted with an otherwise unknown note of the Masora: תחתיו קרי; but this <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> is imaginary.</note> or we must fall in with the strong expression, and this is possible: there is, indeed, no necessity for the subduing to be intended of the use of despotic power, it can also be intended to God-given power, and of subjugating authority. David, the anointed one, but not having as yet ascended the throne, here gives expression to the hope that Jahve will grant him deeds of victory which will compel Israel to submit to him, whether willingly or reluctantly.
entries.c817f2583813c40a5ccc1f883889269cc57d3594: <reference osisRef="Ps.144.3-Ps.144.4">Psa 144:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen10317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10318" type="x-p"/> It is evident that <reference osisRef="Ps.144.3">Psa 144:3</reference> is a variation of <reference osisRef="Ps.8.5">Psa 8:5</reference> with the use of other verbs. ידע in the sense of loving intimacy; חשּׁב, properly to count, compute, here <hi type="italic">rationem habere</hi>. Instead of כּי followed by the future there are consecutive futures here, and בּן־אדם is aramaizingly (בּר אנשׁ) metamorphosed into בּן־אנושׁ. <reference osisRef="Ps.144.4">Psa 144:4</reference> is just such another imitation, like a miniature of Psa 39:6., <reference osisRef="Ps.39.11">Psa 39:11</reference>, cf. Psa 62:10. The figure of the shadow is the same as in <reference osisRef="Ps.102.12">Psa 102:12</reference>, cf. Psa 109:23. The connection of the third stanza with the second is still more disrupt than that of the second with the first.
entries.b78aff5cd404982aa433407063a0f764658ea562: <reference osisRef="Ps.144.5-Ps.144.8">Psa 144:5-8</reference> <div eID="gen10318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10319" type="x-p"/> The deeds of God which Ps 18 celebrates are here made an object of prayer. We see from <reference osisRef="Ps.18.10">Psa 18:10</reference> that ותרד, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.144.5">Psa 144:5</reference></hi>, has Jahve and not the heavens as its subject; and from <reference osisRef="Ps.18.15">Psa 18:15</reference> that the suffix <hi type="italic">em</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.144.6">Psa 144:6</reference> is meant in both instances to be referred to the enemies. The enemies are called sons of a foreign country, i.e., barbarians, as in Psa 18:45. The fact that Jahve stretches forth His hand out of the heavens and rescues David out of great waters, is taken verbatim from <reference osisRef="Ps.18.17">Psa 18:17</reference>; and the poet has added the interpretation to the figure here. On <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.144.8">Psa 144:8</reference></hi> cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.12.3">Psa 12:3</reference>; Psa 41:7. The combination of words “right hand of falsehood” is the same as in Psa 109:2. But our poet, although so great an imitator, has, however, much also that is peculiar to himself. The verb בּרק, “to send forth lightning;” the verb פּצה in the Aramaeo-Arabic signification “to tear out of, rescue,” which in David always only signifies “to tear open, open wide” (one’s mouth), <reference osisRef="Ps.22.14">Psa 22:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.66.14">Psa 66:14</reference>; and the combination “the right hand of falsehood” (like “the tongue of falsehood” in <reference osisRef="Ps.109.2">Psa 109:2</reference>), i.e., the hand raised for a false oath, are only found here. The figure of Omnipotence, “He toucheth the mountains and they smoke,” is, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.104.32">Psa 104:32</reference>, taken from the mountains that smoked at the giving of the Law, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.18">Exo 19:18</reference>; Exo 20:15. The mountains, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.68.17">Psa 68:17</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.76.5">Psa 76:5</reference>), point to the worldly powers. God only needs to touch these as with the tip of His finger, and the inward fire, which will consume them, at once makes itself known by the smoke, which ascends from them. The prayer for victory is followed by a vow of thanksgiving for that which is to be bestowed.
entries.8acf895065233e2f0f81097780e74c41f8e4f7df: <reference osisRef="Ps.144.9-Ps.144.11">Psa 144:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen10319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10320" type="x-p"/> With the exception of <reference osisRef="Ps.108.1-Ps.108.13">Psa 108:1-13</reference>, which is composed of two Davidic Elohim-Psalms, the <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.144.9">Psa 144:9</reference> of this strophe is the only one in the last two Books of the Psalter, and is therefore a feeble attempt also to reproduce the Davidic Elohimic style. The “new song” calls to mind <reference osisRef="Ps.33.3">Psa 33:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.40.4">Psa 40:4</reference>; and נבל עשׂור also recalls <reference osisRef="Ps.33.2">Psa 33:2</reference> (which see). The fact that David mentions himself by name in his own song comes about in imitation of Ps 18:51. From the eminence of thanksgiving the song finally descends again to petition, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.7-Ps.144.8">Psa 144:7-8</reference>, being repeated as a refrain. The petition developes itself afresh out of the attributes of the Being invoked (<reference osisRef="Ps.144.10">Psa 144:10</reference>), and these are a pledge of its fulfilment. For how could the God to whom all victorious kings owe their victory (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.16">Psa 33:16</reference>, cf. 2Ki 5:1; <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.47">1Sa 17:47</reference>) possibly suffer His servant David to succumb to the sword of the enemy! חרב רעה is the sword that is engaged in the service of evil.
entries.730f2349df5611f3970d2c55fb77c97dd728d968: <reference osisRef="Ps.144.12-Ps.144.15">Psa 144:12-15</reference> <div eID="gen10320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10321" type="x-p"/> With reference to the relation of this passage to the preceding, vid., the introduction. אשׁר (it is uncertain whether this is a word belonging originally to this piece or one added by the person who appended it as a sort of clasp or rivet) signifies here <hi type="italic">quoniam</hi>, as in Jdg 9:17; <reference osisRef="Jer.16.13">Jer 16:13</reference>, and frequently. lxx ὢν οἱ υίοὶ (אשׁר בניהם); so that the temporal prosperity of the enemies is pictured here, and in <reference osisRef="Ps.144.15">Psa 144:15</reference> the spiritual possession of Israel is contrasted with it. The union becomes satisfactorily close in connection with this reading, but the reference of the description, so designedly set forth, to the enemies is improbable. In <reference osisRef="Ps.144.12-Ps.144.14">Psa 144:12-14</reference> we hear a language that is altogether peculiar, without any assignable earlier model. Instead of נטעים we read נטעים elsewhere; “in their youth” belongs to “our sons.” מזוינוּ, our garners or treasuries, from a singular מזו or מזוּ (apparently from a verb מזה, but contracted out of מזוה), is a hapaxlegomenon; the older language has the words אסם, אוצר, ממּגוּרה instead of it. In like manner זן, <hi type="italic">genus</hi> (vid., Ewald, <hi type="italic">Lehrbuch</hi>, S. 380), is a later word (found besides only in <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.14">2Ch 16:14</reference>, where וּזנים signifies <hi type="italic">et varia quidem</hi>, Syriac <hi type="italic">zenonoje</hi>, or directly spices from <hi type="italic">species</hi>); the older language has miyn for this word. Instead of אלּוּפים, kine, which signifies “princes” in the older language, the older language says אלפים in Psa 8:8. The <hi type="italic">plena scriptio</hi> צאוננוּ, in which the <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> is even inaccurate, corresponds to the later period; and to this corresponds שׁ = אשׁר in <reference osisRef="Ps.144.15">Psa 144:15</reference>, cf. on the other hand Psa 33:12. Also מסבּלים, laden = bearing, like the Latin <hi type="italic">forda</hi> from <hi type="italic">ferre</hi> (cf. מעבּר in <reference osisRef="Job.21.10">Job 21:10</reference>), is not found elsewhere. צאן is (contrary to <reference osisRef="Gen.30.39">Gen 30:39</reference>) treated as a feminine collective, and אלּוּף (cf. שׁור in <reference osisRef="Job.21.10">Job 21:10</reference>) as a <hi type="italic">nomen epicaenum. </hi> Contrary to the usage of the word, Maurer, Köster, Von Lengerke, and Fürst render it: our princes are set up (after Ezr 6:3); also, after the mention of animals of the fold upon the meadows out-of-doors, one does not expect the mention of princes, but of horned cattle that are to be found in the stalls. זוית elsewhere signifies a corner, and here, according to the prevailing view, the corner-pillars; so that the elegant slender daughters are likened to tastefully sculptured Caryatides - not to sculptured projections (Luther). For (1) זוית does not signify a projection, but a corner, an angle, Arabic Arab. <hi type="italic">zâwyt , zâwia</hi> (in the terminology of the stone-mason the square-stone = אבן פּנּהּ, in the terminology of the carpenter the square), from Arab. <hi type="italic">zwâ , abdere</hi> (cf. e.g., the proverb: <hi type="italic">fı̂'l zawâjâ chabâjâ</hi>, in the corners are treasures). (2) The upstanding pillar is better adapted to the comparison than the overhanging projection. But that other prevailing interpretation is also doubtful. The architecture of Syria and Palestine - the ancient, so far as it can be known to us from its remains, and the new - exhibits nothing in connection with which one would be led to think of “corner-pillars.” Nor is there any trace of that signification to be found in the Semitic זוית. On the other hand, the corners of large rooms in the houses of persons of position are ornamented with carved work even in the present day, and since this ornamentation is variegated, it may be asked whether מחתּבות does here signify “sculptured,” and not rather “striped in colours, variegated,” which we prefer, since חטב (cogn. חצב) signifies nothing more than to hew firewood;<note placement="foot">In every instance where חטב (cogn. חצב) occurs, frequently side by side with שׁאב מים (to draw water), it signifies to hew wood for kindling; wherefore in Arabic, in which the verb has been lost, Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥaṭab</hi> signifies firewood (in distinction from Arab. <hi type="italic">chšb</hi>, wood for building, timber), and not merely this, but fuel in the widest sense, e.g., in villages where wood is scarce, cow-dung (vid., <hi type="italic">Job</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Job.20.6-Job.20.11">Job 20:6-11</reference>, note), and the hemp-stalk, or stalk of the maize, in the desert the Arab. <hi type="italic">b‛rt</hi>, i.e., camel-dung (which blazes up with a blue flame), and the perennial steppe-plant or its root. In relation to Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥaṭab , aḥṭb</hi> signifies lopped, pruned, robbed of its branches (of a tree), and Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥrb ḥâtb</hi> a pruning war, which devastates a country, just as the wood-gathering women of a settlement (styled Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - ḥâťbât</hi> or <hi type="italic">'l - ȟwâṭt</hi>) with their small hatchet (Arab. <hi type="italic">miḥṭab</hi>) lay a district covered with tall plants bare in a few days. In the villages of the <hi type="italic">Merg'</hi> the little girls who collect the dry cow-dung upon the pastures are called Arab. <hi type="italic">bnât ḥâṭbât</hi>, בּנות הטבות. - Wetzstein.</note> and on the other side, the signification of the Arabic <hi type="italic">chaṭiba</hi>, to be striped, many-coloured (IV to become green-striped, of the coloquintida), is also secured to the verb חטב side by side with that signification by Pro 7:16. It is therefore to be rendered: our daughters are as corners adorned in varied colours after the architecture of palaces.<note placement="foot">Corners with variegated carved work are found even in the present day in Damascus in every reception-room (the so-called Arab. <hi type="italic">qâ‛t</hi>) or respectable houses cf. Lane, <hi type="italic">Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians</hi>, Introduction). An architectural ornament composed with much good taste and laborious art out of wood carvings, and glittering with gold and brilliant colours, covers the upper part of the corners, of which a <hi type="italic">ḳâ‛a</hi> may have as many as sixteen, since three wings frequently abut upon the <hi type="italic">bêt el - baḥǎra</hi>, i.e., the square with its marble basin. This decoration, which has a most pleasing effect to the eye, is a great advantage to saloons from two to three storeys high, and is evidently designed to get rid of the darker corners above on the ceiling, comes down from the ceiling in the corners of the room for the length of six to nine feet, gradually becoming narrower as it descends. It is the broadest above, so that it there also covers the ends of the horizontal corners formed by the walls and the ceiling. If this crowning of the corners, the technical designation of which, if I remember rightly, is Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - qrnyt , ḳornı̂a</hi>, might be said to go back into Biblical antiquity, the Psalmist would have used it as a simile to mark the beauty, gorgeous dress, and rich adornment of women. Perhaps, too, because they are not only modest and chaste (cf. Arabic <hi type="italic">mesturât</hi>, a veiled woman, in opposition to <hi type="italic">memshushât</hi>, one shone on by the sun), but also, like the children of respectable families, hidden from the eyes of strangers; for the Arabic proverb quoted above says, “treasures are hidden in the corners,” and the superscription of a letter addressed to a lady of position runs: “May it kiss the hand of the protected lady and of the hidden jewel.” - Wetzstein.</note> <div eID="gen10321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10322" type="x-p"/> The words האליף, to bring forth by thousands, and מרבּב (denominative from רבבה), which surpasses it, multiplied by tens of thousands, are freely formed. Concerning חוּצות, meadows, vid., on Job 18:17. פּרץ, in a martial sense a defeat, <hi type="italic">clades</hi>, e.g., in Jdg 21:15, is here any violent misfortune whatever, as murrain, which causes a breach, and יוצאת any head of cattle which goes off by a single misfortune. The lamentation in the streets is intended as in Jer 14:2. שׁכּכה is also found in Sol 5:9; nor does the poet, however, hesitate to blend this שׁ with the tetragrammaton into one word. The <hi type="italic">Jod</hi> is not dageshed (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.123.2">Psa 123:2</reference>), because it is to be read שׁאדני, cf. מיהוה = מאדני in Gen 18:14. Luther takes <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.144.15">Psa 144:15</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.144.15">Psa 144:15</reference></hi> as contrasts: Blessed is the people that is in such a case, But blessed is the people whose God is the Lord. There is, however, no antithesis intended, but only an exceeding of the first declaration by the second. For to be allowed to call the God from whom every blessing comes his God, is still infinitely more than the richest abundance of material blessing. The pinnacle of Israel’s good fortune consists in being, by the election of grace, the people of the Lord (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.12">Psa 33:12</reference>).  <chapter eID="Ps.144"/> <div eID="gen10322" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 144
This Psalm contains a mixture of praise trod prayer; for David, while he extols in very high terms the great mercies which God had bestowed upon him, is led at the same time, either from a consideration of the many trials to be met with in the whole course of human life, or from the connection he still had with wicked men, to pray that God would continue to show this favor to the end. There is this difference between it and Psalm 18,
The ideas and the phraseology of a considerable part of this Psalm appear to be borrowed from the eighteenth.
that the latter is triumphant throughout, the kingdom having been thoroughly subdued, and affairs going forward prosperously, whereas in the present he mixes up one or two things which are indicative of fear and anxiety, there being some remaining enemies to cause him apprehension.
The occasion on which this Psalm was written can only be conjectured. The Septuagint, Vulgate, Aethiopic, and Arabic versions entitle it “A Psalm of David against Goliah;” and that the Chaldee paraphrast took this to be the subject of the Psalm is evident from his reading in verse 10th, “the sword of Goliah.” Judging, however, from internal evidence, the enemies referred to seem rather to be those of David and his kingdom, after he ascended the throne. Some refer the Psalm to David’s war with the Ammonites and Syrians, recorded in 2 Samuel 10; and it may have been composed by him when about to encounter these hostile powers.
A Psalm of David.
Psalm 144:1-4
1. Blessed be Jehovah, my strength, who teaches my hands for battle, my fingers for war. 2. My goodness, and my munition, my citadel, and my deliverer, my shield, and in him I have hoped, who subdues my people under me. 3. O Jehovah! what is man that thou acknowledgest him? the son of man that thou thinkest of him? 4. Man is like to vanity: his deeds are as a shadow passing away.
 
1. Blessed be Jehovah, my strength
“Ou, mon rocher.” — Fr. marg. “Or, my rock.”
It is very evident that David, since he celebrates the favor of God in such high terms, had not only obtained the kingdom, but gained signal victories. When he calls God his strength, he acknowledges that any courage he had was given him from above, not only because he had been made from a country shepherd a mighty warrior, but because the constancy and perseverance he had shown was signally a gift from God. This term answers better than were we to translate it rock; for, by way of explanation, he adds immediately afterwards, that he had been formed under God’s teaching for war. The words certainly imply an acknowledgment, that though of a warlike spirit, he was not born for warlike enterprises but needed to undergo a change. What kind of a commencement, for example, did he show in the case of Goliah? That attempt would have been preposterous on any other supposition than his being upheld by secret divine support, so as to be independent of mere human help. (1 Samuel 17:40.)
